title: R’ Yehudah ben Dostai
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman cites Makkot 7b: he says in the name of R’ Shimon ben Shatach, “If someone fled from the Land of Israel abroad, his verdict is not overturned.” Hyman reports the Dikdukei Soferim reading: “Dostai son of R’ Yehudah, in the name of R’ Shimon.” Hyman reports that Tosefta Sanhedrin, at the end of chapter 3, reads simply R’ Dostai son of R-Y [בר״י, contextually Yehudah]. Bava Kamma 83b has R’ Dostai ben Yehudah saying: “‘An eye for an eye’ means monetary compensation”; Hyman reports that Dikdukei Soferim cites a manuscript reading R’ Yehudah ben Dostai.

notes.text: The matching checked Makkot passage is on 7a, whereas Hyman supplies 7b. The reversed father-and-son forms in the other readings are retained as reported variants.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier recorded Makkot comparison is at 7a beside supplied 7b; it is inherited, not newly inspected. The fugitive’s verdict is NOT overturned. Dostai son of Yehudah and Yehudah son of Dostai remain Hyman’s reported alternative readings, not one admitted genealogy. His Tosefta and Dikdukei Soferim manuscript claims remain attributed; מכ״י means from a manuscript without a newly identified witness. The abbreviated title in the Tosefta father remains R-Y with a contextual Yehudah lead; other uninspected personal titles stay R’.

Hyman’s print (vol. II, p. 559) gives Makkot 7b. The consulted Makkot 7a has R’ Yehudah son of Dostai in R’ Shimon ben Shatach’s name. It treats flight abroad and flight into the Land of Israel differently. Tosefta Sanhedrin 3:5 in the Machon Mamre edition has R’ Dostai son of R’ Yehudah. At the Bava Kamma 83b passage, Dikdukei Soferim p. 191 gives Dostai son of Yehudah in both main columns and records the reversed Yehudah son of R’ Dostai in a manuscript variant in its notes. At Makkot 7a the Dikdukei Soferim print column has Yehudah son of Dostai in the name of R’ Shimon ben Shatach, while its manuscript column reads Dostai son of R’ Yehudah in the name of R’ Shimon. The editor also points to Yuchasin and the Tosefta. These name forms are preserved at their respective occurrences.
